summary: Washington requires any home sold on or after July 1, 2019 to have at least one smoke alarm, and the seller must install one before the buyer moves in if there isn't one; an owner-occupied single-family home sold after July 26, 2009 must also be equipped with carbon monoxide alarms before the buyer moves in.
alarmType: The sale statute itself only requires at least one smoke alarm and names no power source or sensor technology; devices must meet nationally accepted standards and rules of the chief of the Washington State Patrol through the director of fire protection, and interconnection is expressly not required where it isn't already present in a building being repaired solely as a condition of sale. The residential code rule is stricter for new and permitted work: smoke alarms must be listed to UL 217 (combination smoke/CO alarms to UL 217 and UL 2034) and comply with NFPA 72; they go in each sleeping room, outside each sleeping area near the bedrooms, and on each additional story including basements and habitable attics, at least 3 feet from a bathroom with a tub or shower; multiple alarms in a unit must be interconnected so one sounding sets off all, with listed wireless alarms allowed instead of wiring; primary power must come from the building wiring with battery backup where commercial power is available, but battery-only alarms are allowed in buildings without commercial power and for the alterations/repairs/additions trigger. New attached garages need a heat detector or heat alarm.
coAlarms: Yes, under a separate statute. Residential occupancies generally must have CO alarms under building-code rules; owner-occupied single-family homes legally occupied before July 26, 2009 were exempt, but if such a home is sold on or after July 26, 2009 the seller must equip it with CO alarms meeting the state building code before the buyer or anyone else may legally occupy it. Under the code rule, CO alarms go outside each separate sleeping area in the immediate vicinity of the bedrooms and on each level of the dwelling, per the manufacturer's recommendations, plus inside any bedroom that has a fuel-burning appliance in it or in its attached bathroom.
certification: No inspection or sign-off. No fire department certificate and no seller affidavit is required by the statute. Enforcement happens after the fact: the city fire chief, or the county fire marshal in unincorporated areas, may fine an owner, seller, or tenant up to $200 (up to $5,000 for an owner where a fire then causes damage, injury, or death to a tenant or tenant's household member), and enforcement occurs after a fire when it is evident the home sold on or after July 1, 2019 had no smoke alarm. Failure to comply does not affect transfer of title, ownership, or possession. Licensed real estate brokers are shielded from liability for a seller's non-compliance under both statutes.
citation: RCW 43.44.110 (smoke detection devices in dwelling units; sale provision at (1)(c) and (4)(a)); RCW 19.27.530(2)(b) (carbon monoxide alarms); WAC 51-51-0314 (Residential Code Section R314, smoke alarms and heat detection); WAC 51-51-0315 (Section R315, carbon monoxide alarms)
notVerified: The State Patrol / director of fire protection rules referenced in RCW 43.44.110(2)(b) for smoke device standards were not read, so no state-specific sensor or power-source requirement beyond the statute and the residential code is confirmed.

The residential code requirements in WAC 51-51-0314 and -0315 are triggered by new construction and by permitted alterations, repairs, or additions, not by a sale. WAC 51-51-0315 expressly excepts owner-occupied single-family residences legally occupied before July 26, 2009 from its inspection requirement and points back to RCW 19.27.530(2)(b), so for those homes the CO duty is the seller's at sale. Exactly which code specs a seller must meet when the only trigger is the sale was not resolved by the sources read.
